title: Africa’s Financial Third Way
gist: Rabah Arezki argues the external-finance-leads bargain for African development has broken: Western aid is shrinking, European banks are selling their African franchises, and Chinese sovereign lending has collapsed from a 2016 peak above $28 billion to $2.1 billion in 2024 even as Belt and Road investment surged 254 percent in H1 2026 to a record $33.5 billion in private-equity form. His prescription is for the African Development Bank to abandon direct project lending for a wholesale model — IFC-style A/B syndications, lending through local banks, and reform conditionality to break the sovereign-bank nexus that keeps only 10 percent of sub-Saharan SMEs bank-financed.

themes.theme: The collapse of the external-finance-leads bargain

insights.claim: The decades-long premise that capital from wealthy countries channeled through aid budgets, multilateral banks and private investors would lead African development while Africa followed is now unraveling.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: The core funding assumption behind African sovereign and corporate credit models is being retired — reprice duration risk on the continent accordingly.
insights.locator: For decades, the promise of development finance

insights.claim: Western aid budgets are shrinking, the United States has gutted its development finance ambitions, and European banks are retreating from Africa simultaneously, leaving the continent receiving capital on terms it did not set, in sectors it did not choose, through instruments it cannot control.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Simultaneous withdrawal of three funding channels means the marginal African borrower faces a step-change in cost of capital, not a gradual one.
insights.quote: Africa is increasingly receiving capital on terms it did not set, in sectors it did not choose, through instruments it cannot control.
insights.locator: That promise is now unraveling

insights.claim: As large European banks scale back or sell their African franchises, the African Development Bank is the only remaining institution capable of attracting cross-border capital to the continent at scale.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A single institutional chokepoint now determines whether cross-border capital reaches Africa — concentration risk and, for buyers of European bank divestments, an entry opportunity.
insights.locator: As large European banks have scaled back

themes.theme: China's pivot from state debt to corporate ownership

insights.claim: Chinese lenders provided an estimated $180.9 billion to African governments between 2000 and 2024, which Beijing leveraged into political relationships, U.N. voting blocs, and commercial footholds.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Quantifies the debt stock underpinning China's African political influence — the base from which any restructuring negotiation starts.
insights.locator: Between 2000 and 2024, Chinese lenders provided

insights.claim: New Chinese sovereign lending to Africa peaked above $28 billion in 2016 and fell to just $2.1 billion in 2024, driven by debt distress in Angola, Ethiopia, Ghana, and Zambia.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A 93 percent collapse in the marginal sovereign lender to Africa — the single most important number for African sovereign refinancing risk.
insights.quote: which after peaking above $28 billion in 2016 fell to just $2.1 billion in 2024
insights.locator: Debt distress in Angola, Ethiopia, Ghana, and Zambia

insights.claim: Chinese Belt and Road investments in Africa surged 254 percent year over year in the first half of 2026 to a historic $33.5 billion, with many investments taking the form of private equity in strategic energy, metals, and manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Chinese capital did not leave Africa — it converted from creditor to owner in strategic resource sectors, changing who controls the assets rather than reducing exposure.
insights.quote: But in the first half of 2026, Chinese Belt and Road investments on the continent surged 254 percent from the previous year to a historic $33.5 billion.
insights.locator: Today, however, that model is retrenching

insights.claim: The Chinese instrument in Africa has changed from state loans to corporate ownership but the underlying logic has not, with investment continuing to flow to sectors prioritized in Beijing rather than in Accra or Kinshasa.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Watch equity stakes rather than loan books to track Chinese strategic positioning in African critical minerals and power.
insights.quote: The instrument has changed—from state loans to corporate ownership—but the logic has not
insights.locator: Many of these investments now take the form

insights.claim: China became Africa's default financing alternative because it offered speed and scale that Western finance never had, and did so without the accompanying policy lectures.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Conditionality is a competitive disadvantage in development finance — any Western re-entry strategy has to solve for speed, not just price.
insights.quote: offering the speed and scale that Western finance never had without the lectures
insights.locator: With Western finance failing to show up

insights.claim: The Chinese financing era left Africa with a legacy of debt obligations and foreign control over strategic assets without producing a financing model serving Africa's own development priorities.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Resource nationalism and contract renegotiation risk in African mining and power assets rises as this asymmetry becomes politically salient.
insights.locator: What began as a geopolitical breakthrough

themes.theme: Three failed eras of development finance doctrine

insights.claim: Development finance has cycled through three doctrines — the big push era of the 1950s to 1970s that put infrastructure first, the institutions era of the 1980s and 1990s that put property rights and governance first, and the evidence-based era of the 2000s that put measurement first via randomized control trials and impact investing.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A clean periodization for diagnosing which doctrine a given aid or DFI program is still running on, and therefore its predictable failure mode.
insights.locator: Development finance has long swung

insights.claim: Each development doctrine failed in a characteristic way: infrastructure without functioning institutions produced white elephants, property-rights reforms without political legitimacy generated backlash and instability, and rigorous impact measurement privileged small interventions over the large complex investments that structural transformation requires.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Explains why RCT-driven impact investing systematically under-funds the capital-intensive projects that actually move GDP per capita.
insights.locator: Each idea had its merits

insights.claim: Private capital in Africa flowed to extractive industries such as oil, gas, and minerals where returns were predictable, but steered clear of roads, ports, power grids, and factories.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: The structural gap is non-extractive infrastructure — where risk-sharing instruments, not more capital, are the binding constraint.
insights.locator: Private capital flowed to extractive industries

insights.claim: By the early 2000s Africa was growing faster than at any point in its post-independence history yet still lacked the long-term capital its transformation demanded.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Growth and financing depth decoupled two decades ago — a reminder that African GDP prints do not imply investable capital formation.
insights.locator: By the early 2000s, the continent was growing

themes.theme: The sovereign-bank nexus and SME credit starvation

insights.claim: African banks have shifted away from lending to private borrowers toward financing public fiscal deficits through high-yielding government bonds seen as less risky than credit to individuals in weak economies — rational for banks but ruinous for economic development.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: The sovereign-bank doom loop is the core structural bottleneck; any African financial-sector thesis must model bank asset allocation, not just credit demand.
insights.quote: This may be a rational choice for banks, but it is ruinous for economic development.
insights.locator: Too often, banks have shifted away

insights.claim: Access to finance is the most commonly cited obstacle for SMEs in sub-Saharan Africa, with only 10 percent of surveyed SMEs financed by bank lending and most turning to informal lenders, family networks or retained earnings at effective interest rates that can reach 60 percent.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A 60 percent effective cost of capital versus a 10 percent formal-credit penetration rate defines the size of the addressable market for African fintech lenders.
insights.quote: with only 10 percent of those surveyed financed by bank lending
insights.locator: Surveys find that access to finance

insights.claim: For many African entrepreneurs the cost of capital exceeds the return on productive investment, which itself explains why job creation has lagged so far behind demographic growth.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Africa's employment gap is a financing-cost problem before it is a skills or demand problem — a specific, fixable mechanism.
insights.quote: For many African entrepreneurs, the cost of capital exceeds the return on productive investment
insights.locator: For many African entrepreneurs

insights.claim: When private lending does occur in Africa it often goes to politically connected incumbents and import-trading monopolies rather than to the small- and medium-sized enterprises that create most new jobs.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Credit allocation is captured, so headline credit-to-GDP ratios overstate real private-sector financing depth.
insights.locator: When private lending occurs

insights.claim: Established African banks are insulated from competition by regulatory barriers, licensing restrictions and privileged access to government business, which has slowed the rise of fintech firms capable of delivering cheaper credit to communities banks find unprofitable.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Licensing reform, not technology, is the gating factor for African fintech scale — watch regulators rather than product launches.
insights.locator: Established banks are insulated

insights.claim: Where African fintech has broken through, as with M-Pesa in Kenya or Wave in Senegal, the results have been transformative, but these remain exceptions in a landscape where regulatory incumbency protects the status quo.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Two named proof points define the template; the replication constraint is regulatory permission, so track licensing regimes country by country.
insights.locator: Where fintech has broken through

themes.theme: The AfDB wholesale model: A/B syndication and leverage

insights.claim: The African Development Bank was designed to be the continent's financial architect but has in practice operated largely as a project lender to sovereign borrowers, a model whose balance sheet is too small to substitute for departing capital and which was never built to mobilize private finance at scale.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: The AfDB's current business model cannot fill the gap arithmetically — reform or a permanently smaller African capital pool are the only two outcomes.
insights.locator: This leaves the African Development Bank (AfDB) at a crossroads

insights.claim: The AfDB should adopt the A/B loan structure pioneered by the International Finance Corporation, committing the A portion itself and inviting commercial banks to provide the B portion, so that every billion dollars the bank commits can unlock several billion more in financing.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A concrete multiplier mechanism: leverage rather than balance-sheet expansion is the lever available to a capital-constrained MDB.
insights.quote: The result is that every billion dollars the bank commits can unlock several billion more in financing.
insights.locator: The way to do this is through syndicated loans

insights.claim: Commercial lenders participate in A/B loans because the AfDB's charter-enshrined preferred creditor status means it is repaid ahead of them, and because they can shelter under its tax exemption and its capacity to weather transfer and convertibility risk.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Preferred creditor status is the actual product being sold to private lenders — its erosion would break the entire mobilization model.
insights.locator: Because the AfDB’s charter enshrines it

insights.claim: The AfDB should lend through African financial institutions rather than around them, providing local banks with credit lines, risk-sharing facilities and guarantee schemes absorbing a defined share of losses, conditioned on the money going to productive sectors and SMEs.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Guarantees can redirect the vast pool of savings currently parked in government bonds — the specific mechanism for unwinding the sovereign-bank nexus.
insights.locator: Just as important, the AfDB should lend through

insights.claim: AfDB financing should be conditioned on borrowing states reducing regulatory incentives that favor government bonds over private loans, strengthening insolvency and collateral regimes, closing credit-information gaps, and dismantling barriers protecting banks from competition.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A four-item reform checklist that doubles as a scorecard for which African markets are actually becoming investable.
insights.locator: The AfDB should condition its syndications

insights.claim: The AfDB must keep its own balance sheet strong enough to retain preferred creditor status, price risk properly, and deal decisively with arrears and nonperforming exposures before it can lead this agenda.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: AfDB asset quality is the load-bearing variable for the whole continent's mobilization capacity — watch its arrears disclosures.
insights.locator: To lead this effort, the AfDB must also put its own house in order

themes.theme: The data premium on African capital costs

insights.claim: Investors attach high risk premiums to Africa simply because reliable information is scarce, inflating the cost of capital for the entire continent as investors demand higher returns to compensate for what they cannot measure.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: Part of the Africa risk premium is measurement noise rather than credit risk — an exploitable mispricing for investors who can build proprietary data.
insights.locator: Better economic data would also make a real difference

insights.claim: Filling Africa's chronic statistical gaps with a continental data hub would make investing on the continent both less risky and less expensive.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: A low-cost, high-leverage policy intervention — cheaper than any subsidy and it compresses spreads across every African asset class.
insights.locator: Filling those chronic statistical gaps

insights.claim: Africa needs a new big idea beyond the Western-versus-Chinese binary: private-sector-led transformation financed through Africa's own institutions rather than those in Washington, Brussels, or Beijing.
insights.speaker: Rabah Arezki
insights.so_what: The stated endgame — domestic institutional intermediation — implies growth in African local-currency debt markets and domestic institutional investors.
insights.locator: Facing this landscape, Africa needs a new big idea
